quote: 20.2 Vendor shall also defend, indemnify, and hold harmless the Customer indemnified parties from third-party claims to the extent arising from Vendor's breach of Applicable Law; bodily injury, death, or tangible property damage caused by Vendor; unauthorized access to or disclosure of Customer Data caused by Vendor; or Vendor's gross negligence, wilful misconduct, or fraud.
rationale: Section 20 meets the preferred position in full. Clause 20.1 gives an unqualified Vendor defence and indemnity for third-party IP infringement/misappropriation claims covering Customer, its Affiliates and their personnel; 20.2 adds Vendor's breach of Applicable Law, bodily injury/property damage, unauthorised access to or disclosure of Customer Data caused by Vendor, and Vendor's gross negligence, wilful misconduct and fraud. Clause 20.4 sets out standard procedure (prompt notice with material-prejudice qualifier, cooperation at the indemnifying Party's expense, control of defence, and settlement consent protections). Clause 20.5 provides the infringement remedies (procure, modify/replace, or terminate with refund) as an addition to, not a substitute for, the defence obligation. The Customer indemnity in 20.3 is appropriately narrow — limited to unmodified Customer-supplied material used strictly as authorised and Customer's violation of Applicable Law, with carve-outs for Vendor Technology, modifications, combinations and Vendor instructions. Indemnification obligations are also "Excluded Claims" under 21.3, so the Vendor indemnity is not swallowed by the general liability cap (better than the fallback 3× super-cap). No redline required.

Section 24.4 expressly denies Vendor any right to terminate, suspend, reprice, accelerate Fees, or reduce service on Customer's change of control and requires cooperation with successor administrative changes. Searches for "change of control" and "assign" surface no other trigger; § 9 termination rights are limited to material breach and insolvency, and § 9.2 confirms a lawful reorganization is not itself grounds for termination. Section 13 also lets Customer transfer licence rights to an Affiliate or successor in connection with a Section 24 assignment, and § 30.5 preserves enforcement rights for permitted successors. No redline needed.

proposal.comment: [Playbook] We have expressed the conformance period in numerals and set it at twelve (12) months for software Deliverables (ninety (90) days for all other Deliverables), consistent with our standard 12-month software / 90-day services warranty. We have also clarified that the warranty refund covers all amounts paid for the non-conforming item, because "Fees" is defined in Section 1.5 as the Implementation Fee only, which would leave subscription and service charges unrefundable; if you prefer, we can instead broaden the Section 1.5 definition.

quote: 19.2 For ninety days after delivery or acceptance, whichever is later, each Deliverable will materially conform to its documentation and acceptance criteria. Hosted Services will conform throughout the subscription term.
rationale: Two gaps against the preferred position justify a small redline rather than a clean compliant call. (1) Duration: 19.2 gives every Deliverable only ninety days, spelled out in words. Our preferred position is 12 months for software and 90 days for services, so software Deliverables are short by nine months. Restating the period as "twelve (12) months" for software Deliverables and "ninety (90) days" for all other Deliverables both closes that gap and states the period in numerals/months, removing the ambiguity that caused the period check to fail. Hosted Services already conform throughout the subscription term (twelve-month renewals under 8.2 inside a three-year master term), which we have left untouched. (2) Remedy: 19.4 refunds only "Fees paid for it", and "Fees" is defined in 1.5 as the Implementation Fee alone. As drafted the refund backstop therefore cannot reach subscription or service charges, which materially hollows out the repair/replace/refund remedy the playbook requires; we have tied the refund to all amounts paid for the non-conforming item instead, and offered broadening the 1.5 definition as an alternative. The rest of Section 19 is compliant and unchanged: 19.1 professional and workmanlike plus conformity to documentation and specifications; 19.3 Applicable Law, no malicious code, no functionality diminution, open-source protection; 19.4 re-perform/repair/replace at no charge, non-exclusive for fraud, infringement, confidentiality, privacy, security and indemnified claims; 19.5 disclaims implied warranties only and expressly preserves express warranties, service levels, indemnities and remedies, so it does not swallow the express warranty. Fallback if Vendor resists: retain 90 days for all Deliverables provided the refund fix is accepted.

verification.notes: Deviation call is supported: 19.2 gives only 90 days for all Deliverables (playbook fallback, not preferred 12 months for software), and 19.4's refund is tied to "Fees," which Section 1.5 defines as the Implementation Fee alone — a real defect that hollows out the refund leg of the required repair/replace/refund remedy. Redline is directionally correct and customer-favorable: it extends the period for software Deliverables to twelve (12) months while preserving 90 days for other Deliverables, leaves the already-better Hosted Services subscription-term warranty untouched, and expands the refund to all amounts paid for the non-conforming item. Rule completeness is satisfied: professional-and-workmanlike and documentation conformity (19.1), Applicable Law and no-malicious-code (19.3), and a disclaimer that expressly preserves the express warranties (19.5) are correctly identified as compliant, so no further operations are required. Comment is accurate, correctly cites the 12-month/90-day playbook position, explains the "Fees" definitional problem, and offers a sensible alternative (broadening Section 1.5); tone matches house style. Advisory changed-character ratio on p0080 (0.630) does not indicate over-editing in substance — only the refund phrase within one sentence was touched; the parenthetical "(and not only the Implementation Fee)" is arguably surplus and could be trimmed, and "software Deliverables" is not a defined term given Deliverables exclude Vendor Technology, but neither creates customer risk.

quote: 18.1 Vendor shall maintain, at its own expense throughout the term and for one year afterward, commercial general liability insurance of at least USD 1,000,000 per occurrence and USD 2,000,000 aggregate, workers' compensation as required by law, employer's liability of USD 1,000,000, professional errors and omissions insurance of USD 2,000,000, and cyber and privacy liability insurance of USD 5,000,000.
rationale: Section 18 imposes on Vendor exactly the preferred coverage program: CGL at USD 1M per occurrence / USD 2M aggregate, workers' compensation as required by law (plus employer's liability USD 1M), professional E&O at USD 2M, and cyber/privacy liability at USD 5M (unconditional, which covers Vendor's hosting and processing of Customer Data under Sections 15 and 17), maintained through the term and one year afterward. Section 18.2 adds certificates of insurance on request, reputable insurers, primary coverage, advance notice of cancellation or material reduction, and confirms insurance does not limit Vendor's liabilities. All obligations run against the counterparty and meet or exceed the preferred position, so no redline is warranted.
